title: What is tool calling?
notes: A model can't run code or reach your systems; it can only ask for a tool by name, with arguments.
Your code runs the tool and sends the result back as a tool_result, matched to the request by its id.
Tool calling is a cycle: the model asks, your code runs, the result returns, and the model answers or asks again.

slides.title: What is tool calling?
slides.sub: How a model that can only write text gets real work done
sentences: Welcome to Module 3.
So far Scout can read a question and write a good reply, but it cannot look anything up.
In this lesson you will see how a model asks for a tool, who actually runs it, and how the result gets back.
Halfway through there is a short check, so you know the first half has landed.

slides.title: Talking about an order versus looking it up

left.label: Without tools
points: Ana asks where order ORB-10482 is
Scout has never seen Orbit's order system
It apologises, or worse, it guesses
Leo answers the ticket by hand

right.label: With a tool
points: Scout asks for get_order with ORB-10482
Your code looks the order up
Ana gets her tracking number in seconds

sentences: Start with Ana, who writes in to ask where her new tent is.
Without tools, Scout has a problem: it has never seen Orbit's order system.
It knows plenty about tents and shipping in general, but nothing about Ana's order.
So it apologises, or worse, it guesses, and Leo ends up answering the ticket by hand.
With a tool, Scout can ask for the order to be looked up.
Your code fetches the real status, and Ana gets her tracking number in seconds.

slides.title: So, what is tool calling?
slides.definition: The model asks your code to run a named function with specific arguments, then uses the result in its answer.

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: A doctor writing a lab request. The doctor never runs the test, but reads the result and decides what to do next.

sentences: This is called tool calling, and the whole module rests on it.
The model asks for a tool by name, and fills in the arguments the tool needs.
Your code, not the model, runs that tool.
Then the result goes back to the model, which uses it in its answer.
Think of a doctor writing a request for a blood test.
The doctor never runs the test, but reads the result and decides what to do next.

slides.title: One tool call, message by message

messages.label: Ana
messages.text: Hi, where is my tent? Order ORB-10482.

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: Good news: your Trailhead tent has shipped with ParcelPath. Your tracking number is PP-88213.

aside.label: Notice
aside.text: Scout never touched the order system. It asked, and your code did the work.

sentences: Here is what that looks like in a real conversation.
Ana asks where her tent is, and gives her order number.
Scout does not answer yet; instead it replies with a tool request, get order, with Ana's order number as the argument.
Your code runs the lookup and sends back the result: shipped, with ParcelPath, plus a tracking number.
That result goes back to Scout as a new message in the conversation.
Now Scout writes the reply Ana actually sees, using only facts from the result.
Notice that Scout never touched the order system: it asked, and your code did the work.

slides.title: The tool-calling cycle

center.label: Tool loop
center.sub: repeats until no tool is needed

steps.label: Return
steps.sub: result goes back to the model

note.text: The model chooses the tool. Your code decides what actually runs.

sentences: Every tool call follows the same four steps.
Ask: the model stops and says which tool it wants, and with which arguments.
Run: your code finds the matching Python function and calls it.
Return: your code sends the result back to the model as a tool result.
Answer: the model reads the result and either replies, or asks for another tool.
If it asks again, the cycle goes round once more, and that is how an agent chains several steps together.
The model chooses the tools, but your code decides what actually runs.

slides.title: What your code actually receives
slides.lead: When the model wants a tool, the response tells you so. These are the fields your code reads and writes.

rows.out: The model is waiting for a tool result
This block is the tool request
Your answer, matched to the request by id

aside.label: The id matters
aside.text: Each result carries the id of the request it answers, so two tool calls at once never get mixed up.

sentences: Let us look at what actually arrives in your code.
When the model wants a tool, the response has a stop reason of tool use, which means it is waiting for you.
Inside the response is a tool use block: the request itself.
It holds the tool's name and its input, a small dictionary of arguments.
You answer with a tool result block that repeats the request's id, so the model can match each result to its request.
That id matters most when the model asks for two tools at once.

slides.title: Which jobs need a tool?

note.text: If the answer lives in a system, a file or today's news, the model needs a tool.

sentences: So which jobs need a tool, and which don't?
Writing a friendly reply is pure language, so the model does that well on its own.
Knowing a customer's order status is impossible without a lookup, because the model has never seen your data.
Exact arithmetic is the surprise: models are often close, but close is not good enough for a refund.
Anything recent, like today's carrier delays, comes after what the model learned in training.
And actions, like sending a refund, always need a tool, because the model can only write text.
A good rule: if the answer lives in a system, a file or today's news, the model needs a tool.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: A model can't run code or reach your systems; it can only ask
A tool request names the tool and fills in its arguments
Your code runs the tool and sends back a tool_result with the same id
The cycle repeats: ask, run, return, answer

sentences: Let us pull it together.
A model cannot run code or reach your systems by itself; it can only ask.
A tool request names the tool and fills in the arguments.
Your code runs the tool and sends the result back, matched to the request by its id.
And the cycle repeats, ask, run, return, answer, until the model has what it needs.
Next, you will see how to describe a tool, so the model knows when to use it.

midQuiz.q: Ana asks Scout where order ORB-10482 is. Who actually looks the order up?
options: The model, by connecting to Orbit's order database
Your Python code, after the model asks for get_order
Nobody: the model remembers recent orders from training
midQuiz.explain: The model only writes a tool request. Your code runs the get_order function and sends the result back.
midQuiz.hint: Think of the doctor and the lab request: who writes the request, and who runs the test?

midQuiz.q: Scout's response comes back with stop_reason "tool_use". What should your code do next?
options: Show the response text to the customer
Run the requested tool and send back a tool_result
Send exactly the same request again
midQuiz.explain: tool_use means the model has paused to wait for a result. Run the tool, send the result back, and it carries on.
midQuiz.hint: The model has stopped in the middle of the job. What is it waiting for?

endQuiz.q: Which customer request most needs a tool?
options: Rewrite this reply so it sounds friendlier
What is the status of my order ORB-10533?
Explain what a sleeping bag's temperature rating means
endQuiz.explain: Order status lives in Orbit's system, which the model has never seen. The other two are language jobs it does well alone.
endQuiz.hint: Where does the answer live: in general knowledge, or in Orbit's own data?

endQuiz.q: Scout asks for two tools in one response. How does it know which result belongs to which request?
options: The results must come back in the same order as the requests
Each tool_result carries the tool_use_id of the request it answers
The model works it out from what the results say
endQuiz.explain: Every tool_result repeats the id of its tool_use block, so the model matches them exactly, whatever the order.
endQuiz.hint: Look again at the fields inside a tool_result block.
